pillar_reactions.evidence: Fully converted before the call and reporting results already: 'I put less, I worked less with weights, I did more pull-ups, and I started to work with the [kettle]bells and everything, and I saw the changes, meaning that there were more mobility, for example, the chest wasn't too stiff that I couldn't take my hands to the back, I saw that the shoulders are getting more in shape, which I love.' He also volunteered the pandemic-resilience argument for the modality — 'if God forbid there will be another COVID or whatever, it's shortened the amount of time and the things that you need in order to be in shape' — which is a better pitch than the one he was given.

The rep pitched it lightly and correctly, acknowledging the prospect was already competent: 'it sounds like you're pretty good on it but we'll make it a little bit better... even 5% better makes a big difference.' The prospect agreed on the substance and on the weighting: 'nutrition-wise, I agree with you, super important, it's about 70% of you being able to get your result. I think I'm doing a pretty good work, but maybe as you mentioned, I don't know, maybe five, 7% to get it to, makes a big difference, yeah, I agree with you.' Accepted without questions, but with no incremental value established beyond a 5% improvement on something he already does well.

The only outright objection to a pillar anywhere in this batch, and it went to the offer's central claim. He accepted the mentor framing as valid and then excluded himself from it: 'I think it's very much relevant to people who are less familiar with the exercise kind of a world, because you do need someone to push you, because until it's not becoming part of your routine... But for people who are starting to obtain that kind of routine, they do need a mentor, I less need a mentor, I need more of a coach.' He backed it with evidence — twenty-one years of self-directed training and a prior coach he graduated from in three months. The rep responded only to the vocabulary, agreeing that coach and mentor are much the same thing, and never contested the substance.

anchors.raw: I was following him and other, like, four guys and I reached out to three just to get them standing, know, what's the plan, what's the value. How much it costs, blah, blah, blah, and then to make a calculate decision.
anchors.competitor: Three unnamed kettlebell coaches or creators
anchors.note: A live, structured, three-way competitive tender that the prospect disclosed in his first five minutes. Nobody asked what the others quoted, what they included, or what he liked about them. That is the single most actionable piece of competitive intelligence offered to anyone in this batch and it was left on the floor.

anchors.raw: after COVID, I took for the very first time a professional coach. He didn't come with me to the gym because I don't need it, but we built a plan... we did an Excel for three, four months, and after I understood whatever I need to do, I went by my own.
anchors.note: The definitive anchor on this call. He has already bought exactly this category of service, at what was evidently a far lower price, extracted what he needed in three or four months and left. He then described wanting to repeat that pattern — 'once I understand and train my mind for three months I know that I can take it away.' A six-month, $6,000, accountability-led offer is structurally mismatched to a buyer whose proven behaviour is to buy programming and self-serve. It was never surfaced as an objection because it was never asked about.

anchors.raw: And then that's $200 a month... It's not like you commit to three months. It's monthly rolling at $200 a month.
anchors.note: Second instance in this batch of the rep introducing the company's $200/month tier to a prospect quoted $6,000, and the more consequential of the two because here it was offered as the explicit answer to the price objection and the prospect took it: 'That might be more relevant for me.' Note the composition — three-month foundation-strength-intensity programme, full movement and mobility tutorials, monthly plans mirroring Trevor's own training, and a weekly live class with Trevor. The gap between $200 and $6,000 was never justified on the call.

anchors.raw: if I would have said yes, it would have been the highest training plan I've ever paid in my life
anchors.note: A clean statement of the ceiling and, unusually, offered without hostility — he repeatedly complimented the pricing strategy as correct for the business. The barrier is allocation as a first-year founder rather than affluence: 'I need to understand, you know, how do I allocate my funds, especially with my business as an entrepreneur.' A payment plan was the obvious response and was never mentioned.

anchors.raw: I started to explore, mostly on Instagram and to get familiar with other form of exercises
anchors.note: Fifth consecutive call in this batch where the company's own free content is the primary competitor. Here it is also what rebuilt his training after COVID and what he is currently running kettlebell sessions from.

unmet_demand.want: A granular, front-loaded three-month blueprint with per-exercise technique references that he can execute independently and then own outright
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He described the shape of what he wants in precise detail — a month-by-month progression, links for form on every movement, correct starting weights — and it is a programming product, not a coaching relationship. The core offer is built on six months of ongoing accountability, which is the component he says he does not need. The $200 tier matches him better than the $6,000 one, which is why he took it. This is not a defect in the offer; it is a buyer who wants a different category of product.

unmet_demand.want: To buy components rather than the whole integrated system — 'I would probably take bits and pieces, not everything, because I'm already educated'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme is deliberately not unbundled, as confirmed on the Peter Louis call. Second occurrence of this request in the batch, from the two most experienced prospects in it, which suggests the all-in structure is a live commercial constraint at the top of the market rather than an occasional quibble.

unmet_demand.want: A reason why one-to-one coaching at $6,000 for six months is worth thirty times the self-guided tier
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Never given. The rep described the $200 tier as including a weekly live class with Trevor — thirty minutes training together, thirty minutes Q&A, around twenty people — while the same rep told Luis Ortiz two days earlier that the coaching programme includes no calls at all. On the descriptions actually given to prospects, the cheap tier offers more live founder access than the expensive one. Whichever description is accurate, the value ladder as communicated is inverted.

unmet_demand.want: Assurance that a new modality can be learned without repeating the injury pattern he already has — 'I'm keeping having injuries'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep gave a plausible answer in principle, that the first month is form and technique and that a plan would be built around his imbalances, but he never asked what the injuries actually are, when they occur or whether anything has been diagnosed. The prospect's stated reason for wanting professional guidance is injury avoidance, and it was the least examined thing on the call.
